questions.title: How does the iterative fastText selection pipeline specifically avoid benchmark contamination while maximizing data volume?
questions.question_body: I am reading the 'Data Collection and Decontamination' section and I'm confused about the mechanics of the contamination filter. The paper states they remove any text segment containing a '10-gram string' that exactly matches benchmark substrings. However, mathematical problems often vary slightly (e.g., changing numbers), or benchmarks might be shortened versions of common problems found on the web. If a webpage contains a detailed worked example that is *similar* to a benchmark problem but not identical, will it be filtered out? Conversely, if I just find a 10-gram match on every single math problem on the web, isn't it impossible to collect any 120B tokens without this filter? How does the pipeline balance recall and precision in this specific filtering stage?

questions.title: In the GRPO algorithm, how is the baseline advantage $ ar{r}$ calculated when using Group Relative Advantage Estimation?
questions.question_body: I am studying Equation (2) for the GRPO objective. The text states that advantages $ ar{A}_{i,t}$ are calculated based on relative rewards within each group. It defines outcome supervision as $ ar{A}_{i, t} = 	ilde{r}_i = \frac{r_i- {m mean}(\mathbf{r})}{{m std}(\mathbf{r})}$. However, in Equation (2), there is a summation inside the min/clip function over tokens $t=1$ to $|o_i|$. Since the normalized reward $	ilde{r}_i$ is a single scalar value for the entire output sequence $o_i$, does this mean every token $t$ in that sequence receives the exact same advantage value? How does this differ from PPO where $A_t$ varies per token based on future rewards or value function estimates?

questions.title: Why does training on ArXiv papers seem ineffective for mathematical reasoning according to DeepSeekMath, isn't arXiv full of math proofs?
questions.question_body: In the 'Lessons Learnt in Pre-Training' section, the authors claim that training on ArXiv corpora (like MathPile or ArXiv-RedPajama) shows 'no notable improvements' on benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH, whereas web-scraped data works well. My intuition is that ArXiv contains dense, rigorous mathematical content which should be superior to uncurated web pages. What specific characteristics of industrial-grade math solvers are missing in standard ArXiv preprocessing (LaTeX removals mentioned)? Is it because ArXiv papers focus more on formal proofs and less on step-by-step problem solving demonstrations which benchmarks like MATH require? Or is it purely a matter of data quantity vs quality as implied by the comparison with Common Crawl?

questions.title: How does GRPO handle varying output lengths within a group for advantage estimation?
questions.question_body: When sampling a group $\\{o_1, o_2, \\cdots, o_G\\}$ from Equation (3), these outputs may have different lengths ($|o_i|$ varies). The advantage calculation involves summing over tokens $t$. In PPO with a critic, we usually pre-compute $V(o)$ at the end of each sequence to normalize advantages at each step. GRPO uses relative rewards within the group. If one output in the group has length 100 and another has length 500, how exactly are their token-wise advantages aligned? Does GRPO pad shorter sequences with zero-reward tokens? If so, how does that affect the gradient calculation compared to PPO where we have a specific baseline value function $V_\\psi(o)$?

questions.title: What is the precise definition of 'Process Supervision' versus 'Outcome Supervision' in terms of how $\\hat{A}_{i,t}$ is computed?
questions.question_body: The paper distinguishes between Outcome Supervision RL (OS) and Process Supervision RL (PS) using GRPO. For OS, it says $\hat{A}_{i,t}$ is set to the normalized final reward for all tokens. For PS, it provides rewards at specific indices ($index(j)$). The formula given is $\hat{A}_{i,t} = \sum_{index(j) \ge t} \\widetilde{r}_i^{index(j)}$. This looks like an n-step return or cumulative sum. In standard Reinforcement Learning theory, wouldn't we need a discount factor $\\gamma$ here? The paper doesn't explicitly mention a discount factor in these summations. Is it assumed to be 1 (no discounting)? If so, does this cause instability if reasoning steps are very long chains, effectively giving equal weight to errors near start vs end of computation? Also, how does this differ fundamentally from computing advantages using a learned Value Function in standard RL?
